newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: North Korean children "wasting away", U.N. says.
newsitem.headline: North Korean children "wasting away", U.N. says.

text.p: Tens of thousands of malnourished North Korean children are "wasting away" in the country's three-year-long food crisis and many seemed doomed to die, a senior United Nations official said on Wednesday.

Although this year's rice harvest was shaping up well, it could not provide enough for the communist state to feed its 24 million people without continuing outside help, World Food Programme (WFP) chief Catherine Bertini told reporters.

"Our staff in the country estimates that 50 to 80 per cent of the children they have seen in nurseries are underweight and markedly smaller than they should be for their age. They are literally wasting away," she said.

"We must do more. An entire generation is at risk," Bertini, an American, told a news conference formally launching a new appeal for nearly $46 million in food aid to boost supplies the U.N. is sending for some 2.6 million children under six.

In hospitals visited by WFP staff, only children with medical complications were being treated and those simply malnourished were being sent home. Hospital staff said it was expected many would die, she added.

To back the appeal by the WFP and its fellow Rome-based Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), she distributed photos and film of ailing infants with spindly limbs and distended bellies in nursery schools and hospitals in the capital, Pyongyang.
"This is a case of widespread malnutrition, of a vast number of people who don't have enough to eat. It's now beyond a famine in the making, it's a famine occurring," she declared.

In April, North Korean officials told U.N. representatives in Pyongyang that 134 children had died of malnutrition. But aid agencies believe the actual number is much larger and that adults may now be swlling the death figures.

North Korean officials, whose country long followed a philosophy of self-reliance and had few contacts with the non-communist world, insist that the problem is entirely due to devastating floods and storms over the past three years.

But many analysts say the natural disasters, which hit at harvest time, have only compounded a steady decline in the rigidly state-controlled economy where major resources are poured into maintaining a powerful military machine.
In Seoul on Wednesday, South Korea's central bank said the North's economy shrank in 1996 for the seventh year in a row, largely due to shortages of energy and raw materials.

Gross domestic product fell 3.7 per cent after a 4.6 per cent drop in 1995. Production in manufacturing and most other industries fell sharply, partly due to disruption of transport on the floods which destroyed roads and railway lines.

Bertini said WFP officials visiting North Korean ports had seen ships loaded with scrap metal apparently gathered from the surrounding areas by local authorities to send abroad in the hope of bartering it for food.
These operations were clearly organised by local officials on their own initiative, she added.
Geneva diplomats who follow North Korean affairs said this could be a sign of slackening central authority as foreign trade of any type had always been strictly controlled from Pyongyang.

Bertini said her appeal, covering about 130,000 tonnes of food, was in addition to a $96 million appeal for 206,000 tonnes earlier this year which had been covered by donor governments and organisations.
But even with announced pledges and commercial barter imports, she added, North Korea still faced a food deficit of about one million tonnes this year.
